candidates.title: The title is a Ferris Bueller joke, and the film is in the episode
candidates.detail: The episode title riffs on John Hughes's 'Ferris Bueller's Day Off' (1986). It is not just a pun on the title: the film is used inside the episode as the tool that finally makes the team's clique problem legible to Ted. Alice first tries to explain the three groups through the Harry Potter trio and it fails, because Ted has never read the books; Beard re-translates the same structure through Ferris Bueller and it lands. The film's most-quoted line is the school secretary running through every tribe at the high school and reporting that all of them adore Ferris — i.e. a catalogue of cliques, and one person who moves freely between all of them. That is a fairly exact description of what Ted is trying to become for this squad. IMPORTANT FOR THE REVIEWER: confirm (a) that the title is being read as a Ferris Bueller nod by more than one outlet and not just inferred, and (b) that the Harry Potter / Ferris Bueller exchange actually happens on screen.

candidates.title: Mixing the cliques into quiz teams is a textbook superordinate goal
candidates.detail: The squad has fractured into three position-based cliques. Ted's fix is not a speech and not simply 'spend time together' — he puts them into quiz teams that cut across the cliques, so that winning requires people who dislike each other to pool what they each happen to know. That is precisely the mechanism Muzafer Sherif isolated in the 1954 Robbers Cave study: two hostile groups of boys were NOT reconciled by contact or shared social events, which is the part usually forgotten. What worked was a 'superordinate goal' — a task beyond the resources of either group alone (unblocking the camp water supply, freeing a stuck truck, pooling money for a film). By the end, roughly two-thirds of the boys' friendship choices crossed the old group line. The episode is running the same experiment with a pub quiz. Sherif's paper: 'Superordinate Goals in the Reduction of Intergroup Conflict', American Journal of Sociology 63(4), 1958.

candidates.title: What actually fuses them is a common enemy — the fast fix, not the durable one
candidates.detail: The quiz mixes them, but the thing that visibly welds the squad together is a group of sexist men at the pub: the players unite against a shared adversary, win, and the night ends in a brawl and a cell. Sherif also tested this — the 'common enemy' method — and treated it as an expedient rather than a solution, because uniting two groups against a third does not dissolve the conflict, it just relocates it upward into a bigger one. So the episode arguably shows both mechanisms in one night: the durable one (a shared task nobody can win alone) and the cheap one (someone to be against), with the cheap one getting the cheer. IMPORTANT FOR THE REVIEWER: the superordinate-goal finding is solidly sourced; Sherif's specific caution about the common-enemy method is the part I could only reach through secondary summaries because the primary text 403'd. If a second independent source for that caution cannot be opened, this should be scored down or dropped rather than softened — the point only works if the caution is really Sherif's.

candidates.title: The trailblazer is played by an actual trailblazer
candidates.detail: Zelda Southport, the investor who turns up as keynote speaker at the Women's Football Business Summit, calls out the men in the room for shallow support of women's sport, and later quietly bails the arrested squad out, is played by Tracey Ullman. Brendan Hunt has said the writers first imagined a younger executive, then realised an older woman would give Rebecca something she has almost never had on this show — a female mentor — and that once they settled on that, Ullman was the only name they considered. The casting rhymes with the part: 'The Tracey Ullman Show' ran on Fox from April 1987 to May 1990, was the first Fox primetime series to win an Emmy, and won ten in all. Ullman is described as the first British woman offered her own sketch show in the United States. And the animated Simpsons shorts that ran inside her show were spun off into the longest-running American primetime scripted series.

candidates.title: Three teen-movie solutions, all rejected on the grounds of homicide
candidates.detail: Brainstorming how to break up cliques, Ted and Beard run through the films that have already answered the question — 'Mean Girls', 'Heathers' and 'The Lost Boys' — and rule each out because the method in each case is, respectively, vehicular manslaughter, serial murder and a stake through the heart. It is a decent joke about how much of the cultural canon on cliques is actually about killing people, and it also quietly places the episode in a lineage: Janis's hand-drawn cafeteria map in 'Mean Girls' (written by Tina Fey, 2004) is the definitive pop-culture diagram of a room divided into tribes, which is exactly what Alice has to draw for Ted. IMPORTANT FOR THE REVIEWER: the three-film list comes from one recap so far — corroborate before including.

candidates.title: Sharon Fieldstone is back, and the subject is now her field
candidates.detail: Dr Sharon Fieldstone (Sarah Niles) returns, appearing on Trent's podcast to talk about how cliques wreck a dressing room — reportedly now working as an academic with a book on locker-room culture. The shape of that is worth noticing. Sharon was hired in the season-two premiere, 'Goodbye Earl', for one narrow job: Dani Rojas had the yips after a penalty killed the club's dog. By the end of that episode other players were quietly queueing at her door. The club brought her in as a patch and she turned out to be the thing the club was missing. Four seasons on, the specific problem Ted is facing is literally what she now writes about — the show's answer to a coach who cannot get into the dressing room is the person who taught him the inside of his own head. IMPORTANT FOR THE REVIEWER: verify the 'professor' and 'book' details specifically; they come from recaps rather than anything primary.

candidates.title: It is the same knee
candidates.detail: Roy's knee gives out during his run of dates, sending him for a scan. That knee has a history and a date. In the season-one finale, 'The Hope That Kills You', Roy came on against Manchester City, chased down Jamie Tartt to stop him scoring, and wrecked his knee doing it — the injury that ended his playing career, with commentators wondering aloud on the night whether that was his last game. The joke of this episode is that the injury he took for a football club, in the act of stopping the boy he could not stand, is now the thing that interrupts him trying to win Keeley back. Careers end; the knee stays. NOTE FOR THE REVIEWER: the app already carries a card on that injury at S1E10 (s1e10-roy-kent-last-stand-injury) and an S1E9 card on Roy being benched. This card is only worth including if it is clearly about the recurrence rather than re-telling the original injury.

candidates.title: Roy tries to speedrun ten dates and that is the whole character note
candidates.detail: Keeley's condition for trying again is that Roy go on ten proper dates with other people first, so that choosing her is a choice rather than a default. Roy responds by booking the dates back-to-back in one venue — treating a test designed to measure sincerity as a fixture list to be cleared. He then has a genuine, unplanned connection with a barmaid, which is the only part of the night that was not scheduled. It is a neat statement of Roy's lifelong problem: he is excellent at effort and terrible at openness, and the exercise only works on the one occasion he stops running it as an exercise. NOTE FOR THE REVIEWER: Alan Sepinwall's review calls this one of the worst sitcom plots ever and criticises season four's padding, particularly of its women — worth weighing before this ships as an admiring card.

candidates.title: A night at the pub is a defensible coaching decision, not a soft option
candidates.detail: Ted cancels training to take the squad drinking, which reads as the sitcom answer. The sports-science literature is friendlier to it than you would expect. Carron, Colman, Wheeler and Stevens's 2002 meta-analysis 'Cohesion and Performance in Sport' (Journal of Sport and Exercise Psychology 24(2), 168–188) pooled 46 studies and 164 effect sizes and found a moderate-to-large relationship between cohesion and performance, and the field distinguishes task cohesion (commitment to the shared job) from social cohesion (liking each other) — with the practical upshot reported as both task-oriented and social-oriented team-building being worth doing. That does not make Ted right about the brawl. It does mean the thing he cancelled training for is a measured variable rather than a vibe. candidates.title: The cliques are drawn along positional lines
candidates.detail: The squad has not split by age, nationality or seniority — the three groups are the midfielders, the defenders and the attackers, and the recaps describe them in the terms football uses about those positions anyway: the midfielders as the logical ones, the defenders as protective and anxious, the attackers as thrilling and selfish. That is a real piece of the sport's folk psychology being used as characterisation: the shape a coach draws on a whiteboard has hardened into three social groups who will not eat together. It also makes the problem structurally different from the men's-team problems Ted solved before, which were mostly about individuals.

candidates.title: Ted's best tool is a room he is not allowed into
candidates.detail: Almost everything Ted has ever fixed, he fixed in a dressing room — the biscuits, the suggestion box, the speeches, the reading of a mood before anyone says anything. Coaching a women's team, he cannot walk in, so the information reaches him second-hand through Alice Chilton, and by the time he acts on it the cliques have set. It is the season's quiet structural joke: the obstacle is not a villain and not a budget line this time but a doorway, and his response is to invent a dressing room somewhere else, which is what the pub turns out to be.
